extracted.intended_audience: junior/senior undergraduate mathematics students and instructors of introductory mathematical logic
extracted.subtask_description: A textbook-level presentation of sentential, first-order, and some second-order topics in mathematical logic aimed at undergraduate courses (quarter- or semester-length), emphasizing proofs, truth, and computability and giving flexible paths for instructors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three-part description of a formal language
rubrics_metrics.description: To describe a formal language we will generally give three pieces of information: (1) the set of symbols (the alphabet); (2) the rules for forming the 'grammatically correct' finite sequences of symbols (well-formed formulas); (3) the allowable translations between English and the formal language.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Only in the third part is any meaning assigned to the wffs. One may manipulate wffs knowing only the alphabet and formation rules, but translations assign semantic content and guide the development. When giving this description, be explicit about which symbols are logical (connectives, parentheses) and which are nonlogical (sentence/parameter symbols).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer decomposition into atomic parts (use operators rather than new atomic symbols)
rubrics_metrics.description: Prefer to break sentences down into atomic parts as much as possible (example: represent 'not K' as (¬ K) rather than inventing a new symbol J).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This encourages compositional analysis: given truth/falsity of atomic parts one can compute truth/falsity of compounds. Examples in the text show translations (K, C, (¬C), (C ∧ K), (K → (¬C))). The anti-pattern is inventing fresh atomic symbols for compound meanings, which obscures structure and prevents compositional truth-calculation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compositionality / truth-functional connectives
rubrics_metrics.description: Compound sentences should be constructed so that, whenever we are given the truth or falsity of the atomic parts, we can immediately calculate the truth or falsity of the compound (use sentential connectives ¬, ∧, ∨, →, ↔ and truth tables).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construct and use truth tables (Table I illustrates this). The text emphasizes that this calculability of compound truth from atomic truth is an important aspect of the decompositions made for compound sentences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alphabetic/symbol design: no symbol is a finite sequence of other symbols
rubrics_metrics.description: Assume that no one symbol is a finite sequence of other symbols; i.e., symbols are atomic and not themselves finite concatenations of other symbols.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This technical requirement guarantees unique decomposability/readability of finite sequences (see Lemma 0A and related remarks). Anti-patterns such as treating 'A3' as equal to a sequence like (¬, A4, () are disallowed. Ensures that if two sequences of symbols are equal, they have the same length and corresponding symbols.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choices for sentence-symbol schemes
rubrics_metrics.description: One may use infinitely many distinct sentence symbols (A1, A2, ...) or a single symbol with primes (A, A', A'', ...) or an arbitrary set of sentence symbols; each choice has tradeoffs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text notes the smaller-symbol advantage of the prime scheme (fewer distinct symbols) but also that allowing arbitrary sets of sentence symbols (countable or not) is possible; some later results (e.g., Section 1.7) are affected by this choice. Instructor or language designer should pick the scheme suited to the intended scope and later technical needs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish logical vs nonlogical symbols and fix roles of connectives
rubrics_metrics.description: Treat sentential connective symbols (¬, ∧, ∨, →, ↔) and parentheses as logical symbols whose role never changes, while sentence symbols are parameters/nonlogical symbols whose translations are open to interpretation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When giving translations between English and the formal language, keep the role of connectives fixed; sentence symbols map to declarative English sentences but their particular meaning is left flexible to allow different interpretations/models.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pedagogical organization and flexibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Make material accessible to typical undergraduate students; organize the book to be flexible for different course lengths and instructor choices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use footnotes at the start of sections to indicate optional paths for instructors or independent readers. The book is designed to fit quarter or semester courses: with a quarter one typically reaches models of first-order theories (Section 2.6); a semester allows coverage of undecidability (Section 3.0) and in a second term Chapter 3 can be covered more fully.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exercise conventions for textbook usage
rubrics_metrics.description: Exercises are given at the end of nearly all sections. If an exercise bears a boldface numeral, the results of that exercise are used in the exposition; unusually challenging exercises are marked with an asterisk.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This convention helps instructors and readers identify which exercises are essential to the text's development and which are optional or harder; place exercises adjacent to the relevant material and use clear typographic markers for dependence and difficulty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pedagogical balance for induction and recursion
rubrics_metrics.description: Present induction and recursion with a more extensive discussion than customary: provide an informal account in lectures and a precise version in the book.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author prefers that lectures give intuition while the book supplies a precise formal statement; Section 1.4 receives expanded treatment to support this approach.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parsing algorithm and unique readability
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide parsing algorithms (for sentential logic and for first-order logic) and establish unique readability of terms and formulas so that well-formedness and parsing are decidable and unambiguous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text includes parsing algorithms (Sections 1.3 and 2.3) and a discussion of unique readability; implementations of formal languages or tooling should follow similar algorithms to guarantee that any well-formed string has a unique parse tree and that parsing is effective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Model construction principle: select relevant features
rubrics_metrics.description: When constructing a model of some real-life or mathematical situation, select some features of the original object to represent (the 'essential' ones) and ignore others (the 'irrelevant'); the model's success depends on this selection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use illustrative examples (airplane: shape vs size; mathematical deductions: form over content). The book emphasizes that whether the model meets its purpose depends largely on the choice of properties to be represented; this guides the design of languages and semantics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explicitly state scope and limitations of the formal language
rubrics_metrics.description: Acknowledge that formal languages trade expressive breadth for precision: they escape natural-language ambiguity but have sharply limited expressiveness; certain logical systems (many-valued, modal, intuitionistic) are outside the book's scope.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Set reader expectations clearly: explain what will and will not be covered, and indicate that choices (e.g., two models: sentential vs first-order) are motivated by differing expressive needs; include examples demonstrating expressiveness limits.
